paragraphs.source_en: This is still a very good positioning idea. "Margarine" has always been perceived as imitation butter. Since you can't change a mind once a mind is made up, a better strategy to overcome a negative is to change the name. "Soy butter" is real butter, only it's made from soy beans and not cow milk. Take margarine, for example. Even though the product has been around for decades, it is still perceived as imitation butter. (It's not nice to fool Mother Nature.) A better choice of name at the beginning would have helped. What should margarine have been called? Why "soy butter," of course.

paragraphs.source_en: The psychological problem with a name like "margarine" is that it is deceptive. It hides the origin of the product. Everyone knows that butter is made from milk. But what's margarine made from? Because the origin of the product is hidden, the prospect assumes there must be something basically wrong with margarine. Bringing the Product Out of the Closet The first step in overcoming negative reactions is to bring the product out of the closet. To deliberately polarize the situation by using a negative name like soy butter. That allows the development of a longterm program to sell the advantages of soy butter versus cow butter. An essential ingredient of such a program is "pride of origin" which the soy name connotes. (As does peanut butter, for that matter.) The same principle is involved in the shift from colored to Negro to black.
